steps.decision: List the five letters first and fill in what you are given. Written out like this, the choice of formula stops being a guess.

steps.working: $v = u + at$ leaves out $s$, which is the letter not wanted here.
steps.decision: Two letters are unknown, so pick the formula that misses out the one the part does not ask for. Here that is $s$.

options: Because the part asks for a and does not need s
Because v = u + at is the first formula on the sheet
Because s is always left out when t is known
whyMenu.explain: Three of the five letters are known and one more is wanted, so choose the formula that contains those four and no others. Nothing about the order on the sheet matters.

steps.decision: Substitute, then rearrange. Writing the substitution line before the rearranged one is what earns the method mark even if the algebra then slips.
This one leaves out $a$. Using it keeps the answer clear of the acceleration just found, so a slip there cannot travel into this part.
Work out the bracket first, then halve, then multiply. The answer carries its unit: metres, because a displacement is a length.

twin.stem: A go-kart starts from rest and accelerates uniformly in a straight line to 12 m/s in 5 seconds. Calculate the distance it travels in those 5 seconds.

items.skill: Prerequisite: make a letter the subject of a formula
items.stem: From an earlier topic: Rearranged so that $a$ is the subject, $v = u + at$ becomes which of these?

options.feedback: Take $u$ from both sides, then divide both sides by $t$.
Only the whole of the left-hand side may be divided by $t$, not one term of it. Subtract $u$ first.
The $t$ is multiplying $a$, so it is undone by dividing, not by subtracting.
Multiplying by $t$ undoes a division. Here $a$ was multiplied by $t$, so divide.

items.skill: Prerequisite: solve a linear equation with a bracket

options.feedback: Divide both sides by 4 to get $U + 26 = 36$, then take 26 off.
The 26 has been taken off 144 and the multiplication by 4 never undone: $144 - 26 = 118$. Divide by 4 first, giving $U + 26 = 36$.
That treats $4(U + 26)$ as $4 \times 26 \times U$. The bracket is a sum, so it cannot be turned into a product.
That is $U + 26$, which is one step from the answer. Take the 26 off to finish.

items.skill: Prerequisite: substitute with a square and a half
items.stem: From an earlier topic: Work out $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.8 \times 6^{2}$.

options.feedback: $6^{2} = 36$, then $0.8 \times 36 = 28.8$, and half of that is 14.4.
The 6 has not been squared: that is $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.8 \times 6$.
The squaring and the multiplication are right, but the half has not been applied.
That squares the whole of $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.8 \times 6$: $2.4^{2} = 5.76$. The square belongs to the 6 alone, so work out $6^{2} = 36$ first.

items.skill: Choose the formula that leaves out the letter you do not need
items.stem: A body has a known starting velocity, a known acceleration and a known final velocity. You need the distance. Which formula should you choose?

options.feedback: You know $u$, $v$ and $a$ and you want $s$. This is the formula that leaves out $t$, the letter you neither know nor need.
That one leaves out $s$, which is the very thing you are looking for.
It would work if you knew $t$, but you do not, so it brings in a second unknown.
Again this needs $t$. Choose the formula whose missing letter is the one you do not have.

items.skill: Turn a deceleration into a signed acceleration
items.stem: A car travelling in the positive direction decelerates at 3 m/s². What goes in the formula for $a$?

options.feedback: Slowing down while travelling forwards means the velocity is falling, so the acceleration is negative.
That would make the car speed up. A deceleration is a negative acceleration once the direction of travel is positive.
The size does not change, only the sign. The deceleration is 3 m/s², so $a = -3$.

options.text: It depends on whether $u$ is positive
options.feedback: Once the direction of travel is taken as positive, slowing down is always a negative acceleration.

items.skill: Substitute into s = ut + half a t squared
items.stem: A trolley starts at 3 m/s and accelerates uniformly at 0.8 m/s² for 6 seconds. Which line is the correct substitution into $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^{2}$?

options.feedback: The $t$ inside the second term is squared and the $t$ in the first term is not. That gives 32.4 m.
The 6 in the second term has not been squared, which is the slip the Summer 2019 examiners singled out on this formula.
Only the second term carries the $t^{2}$; the first term is $ut$, so it cannot be pulled inside the same bracket.
The squares are on the wrong terms: $u$ multiplies $t$, and $\tfrac{1}{2}a$ multiplies $t^{2}$.

items.skill: Refuse to assume a middle point is the midpoint
items.stem: Points P, Q and R lie on a straight line, with PR = 144 m. A particle passes all three. Nothing in the question says where Q is. What is the distance PQ?

options.text: Not yet known: it has to be worked out from the motion
options.feedback: Q is wherever the velocities put it. Work out the time or the velocity at Q first, then the distance.
Nothing says Q is halfway. The Summer 2025 examiners reported weaker candidates assuming exactly this and setting the distance to half.

options.text: 144 m, because P and R are 144 m apart
options.feedback: That is the whole of PR. PQ is only part of it.

options.text: It cannot be found at all
options.feedback: It can: the velocity at Q, with $u$ and $a$, is enough to fix it.

parts.stem:
Points P, Q and R lie on the same straight line, in that order. The distance PR is 144 m.
A particle moves with constant acceleration. It passes P with a velocity of $U$ m/s and, 8 seconds later, passes R with a velocity of 26 m/s.

Calculate the value of $U$.

Answer ________
hints: You know $s$, $v$ and $t$ and you want $u$.
That is the formula which leaves out $a$.
Keep the bracket: $U + 26$ is a sum, not a product.

commonErrors.feedback: The bracket has become a product: $U + 26$ has been treated as $26U$. The formula and the substitution are right, so the method mark (M) is safe; keep the bracket and divide by 4 instead. The Summer 2025 examiners reported this exact line.

parts.stem:
Calculate the acceleration of the particle.

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: You now know $u$, $v$ and $t$.
Use $v = u + at$.
parts.workedSolution: $v = u + at$ gives $26 = 10 + 8a$, so $8a = 16$ and $a = 2$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That is the average of the two velocities, which is a velocity in m/s rather than an acceleration in m/s². Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time.

parts.stem:
The particle passes Q with a velocity of 18 m/s.

Calculate the time taken by the particle to move from P as far as Q.

Answer ________ s
hints: From P to Q you know $u$, $v$ and $a$ and you want $t$.
Use $v = u + at$ again, with the velocity at Q as $v$.

commonErrors.feedback: That comes from treating Q as the halfway point and using $s = 72$. Nothing in the question puts Q in the middle; the velocity at Q is what fixes its position.

parts.stem:
Calculate the distance QR.

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: v squared = u squared + 2as chosen with u = 18 and v = 26

hints: From Q to R you know $u = 18$, $v = 26$ and $a = 2$.
You do not need the time, so use the formula that leaves $t$ out.
Check at the end: PQ and QR should add to 144 m.

commonErrors.feedback: That is half of PR, which assumes Q is the midpoint. The Summer 2025 examiners reported weaker candidates doing exactly this. Work QR out from the velocities at Q and R.
The $u^{2}$ term has been dropped, so this is the distance from rest to 26 m/s. The particle is already travelling at 18 m/s at Q, and that 324 has to be subtracted.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh is finding how far a trolley travels. It starts at 3 m/s and accelerates uniformly at 0.8 m/s² for 6 seconds. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The list and the choice of formula are both right. Line 3 writes the second term as $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.8 \times 6$ instead of $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.8 \times 6^{2}$: the $t$ inside that term is squared, and only that one is.
findTheMistake.feedback: Listing the letters and naming the formula is exactly the method the scheme rewards, and that method mark (M) is safely earned. The working mark (W) goes with the squared $t$. The Summer 2019 examiners named this as one of the two arithmetic slips they saw most on this formula, the other being a bracket expanded wrongly.

prompts.prompt: What is the first thing to write in any constant-acceleration question?
prompts.answer: The list: s, u, v, a, t, with the values you are given filled in and a question mark beside the one you want.

prompts.prompt: Which constant-acceleration formula leaves out the displacement?
prompts.answer: v = u + at. It links the two velocities, the acceleration and the time.

prompts.prompt: Which constant-acceleration formula leaves out the time?
prompts.answer: v squared = u squared + 2as. Use it when no time is given and none is wanted.

prompts.prompt: A body decelerates at 3 m/s². What goes into the formula for a?
prompts.answer: Minus 3, once the direction of travel has been taken as positive. A deceleration is a negative acceleration.

prompts.prompt: In s = ut + half a t squared, which t is squared?
prompts.answer: Only the one in the second term. The first term is u multiplied by t, with no square.

prompts.prompt: Three points lie on a line and the question names all three. What must you not assume?
prompts.answer: That the middle one is halfway. Its position comes from the velocities, not from the picture.
